distinct_values: Cache‑Pressure Gate Advantage Test
Gate advantage under cache pressure on low‑memory targets
Gate‑CPU‑scaling‑on‑target‑hardware
Gate‑advantage under cache‑pressure on target hardware
Gate‑advantage under target‑device cache constraints
A Silero‑VAD gate will retain at least a 5× CPU‑usage reduction on a Pi‑class device (Raspberry Pi 4, 1 MiB L2 cache) despite cache pressure and real‑world audio content.
On a Pi‑class device with ≤1 MiB L2 cache, the Silero‑VAD gate still yields ≥2× CPU reduction without increasing false‑positive hum detection.
On a Pi‑class device with ≤256 KB L2 cache, the Silero‑VAD gate will not retain its >10× CPU‑usage advantage over the ungated watcher.
On a device with limited L2 cache (e.g., Raspberry Pi 4), the Silero‑VAD gate will still reduce CPU usage by at least a factor of 2 compared to the ungated watcher.
Under cache‑pressure conditions the Silero‑VAD gate retains at least a 10 × CPU‑usage advantage over the ungated watcher on target low‑resource hardware.

Run the full watcher pipeline on a Raspberry Pi 4 with and without the Silero gate using the same three audio fixtures (steady hum, fan noise, real speech) for 30 s each. Measure per‑second CPU usage via `resource.getrusage`, record wall‑clock latency, and log gate pass‑through rate for the hum fixture. Repeat each condition 5 times (sessions) with thread pinning (OMP/BLAS = 1).

Run the watcher on a 30 s audio clip (mixed speech + 150 Hz hum) on a Raspberry Pi 4 (1 MiB L2, no L3). Measure CPU core percent for (a) ungated watcher, (b) gated watcher. Perform three conditions: (i) warm run (no cache flush), (ii) cold run (flush L1/L2 before each 100 ms chunk), (iii) increased working‑set run (process 4 MiB of unrelated data between chunks to force cache eviction). Use `resource.getrusage` for CPU time and wall‑clock for sanity check. Repeat each condition for 5 sessions (different audio seeds) to obtain session‑level samples.

Run the watcher on a Raspberry Pi 4 (2 MiB L2, 4 MiB L3) processing the same six benchmark signals (steady hum, fan, keyboard, music triad, white noise, near‑silence) for 30 s each. Measure CPU time via getrusage for (a) ungated watcher, (b) gated watcher, (c) a minimal YIN‑only baseline. Record warm runs (no cache flush) and cold runs (L1/L2/L3 flushed before each 100 ms chunk). Compute the ratio (ungated / gated) for both warm and cold conditions.

Run the watcher on a representative 30 s audio clip (including 150 Hz and 200 Hz hum) on the target device in two conditions: (1) ungated, (2) gated. Measure (a) CPU core‑percentage via getrusage, (b) fraction of frames where the gate clears the frame (frac), and (c) emitted F0 error compared to reference. Use three independent sessions (different random seeds for audio ordering).

Run the watcher on a representative 30 s audio clip (same six signals as ADOPTION‑PLAN) on the target device in three conditions: (1) ungated, (2) gated, (3) gated with a cold‑flush before each 100 ms chunk (L1/L2/L3 flushed). Measure CPU time using `resource.getrusage` (utime+stime) and wall‑clock time for each session; repeat for 5 independent sessions (different random seeds for the gate).
Cold‑flush control (L1/L2/L3 cleared) to expose worst‑case cache behaviour. | L1‑resident baseline loop (32 KiB buffer) to confirm the measurement pipeline works under the same flush conditions.
Cold‑flush run (L1/L2/L3 flushed before each 100 ms chunk) to isolate cache effects | Synthetic audio with no hum (silence) to confirm gate does not add overhead when not needed

Warm run without cache flush (baseline for each fixture). | Cold run with L1/L2/L3 flush before each 100 ms chunk (to expose worst‑case cache pressure). | Synthetic silence‑only audio to verify that the gate does not fire spuriously.

Warm ungated watcher (baseline CPU cost). | Cold ungated watcher (verifies that cache flushing alone does not create advantage). | Synthetic no‑gate control: a dummy pass‑through that does no VAD but processes the same audio length (verifies measurement pipeline).
Warm ungated watcher (baseline) | Cold ungated watcher (cache‑flush control) | Warm gated watcher (experimental) | Cold gated watcher (cache‑flush control)
Gated CPU usage is ≤ 1.0 × the ungated usage (no reduction) or the gate fails to suppress the hum (gate pass‑through > 5 %).
No difference in CPU usage between gated and ungated runs (ratio ≈ 1) and/or hum‑frac > 0.05
No measurable CPU reduction (ratio ≤ 1.5×) between gated and ungated runs.
Ratio of ungated to gated CPU usage ≤ 1 (no advantage or inversion).
The gated watcher shows no CPU‑usage advantage over the ungated watcher (ratio ≤ 2).
If gated CPU usage is ≥80 % of ungated or hum‑frac exceeds 0.01, abandon the gate for this hardware class.
If the gated run uses > 50 % of a core or the hum pass‑through exceeds 5 %, the hypothesis is falsified and the gate is deemed unsuitable for target hardware.
If the gated watcher’s CPU usage is ≥ 80 % of the ungated usage (ratio ≤ 1.25×) or the cold‑flush makes the gated version slower than ungated, the hypothesis is falsified.
If the measured ratio is ≤ 1 in either warm or cold runs, the hypothesis is falsified and the gate cannot be relied upon for low‑memory devices.
If the ratio is ≤ 2 in any session, or the median ratio across sessions ≤ 5, the hypothesis is abandoned and the gate is deemed unsuitable for low‑resource devices.

evidence_claims: The current VAD watcher (`watcher.py`) classifies steady‑state non‑speech signals as speech at a saturated rate of ~89 % of frames.
A 2.2 MiB Silero‑VAD gate placed before the watcher reduces CPU usage by roughly 18 × on the development workstation.
When the L1/L2/L3 caches are flushed before each 100 ms chunk, the gated watcher becomes ~19 × slower than the ungated watcher (cold vs warm cost).
The character‑delta representation (ASCII‑motion) does **not** measure subject motion; the flip‑rate is driven by camera auto‑exposure drift.
Per‑frame gain normalisation does **not** reduce drift; the reported 50 × reduction was an arithmetic illusion.
Row‑band removal combined with a 3‑frame temporal median reduces the occupied‑room flip‑rate from 2.99 % to 0.14 % (≈21 × improvement) while SNR remains ~1.85 (no gain).
The Silero‑VAD gate does **not** under‑report its peak by 14.5 ×; the earlier claim was based on mismatched intervals.
F0 jump size predicts speaker change only for the *children* cell (Spearman ρ = 0.341, p = 0.0061 after Bonferroni correction); all other cells show no significant effect.
Multimodal LLMs can detect speaking from a 160×96 webcam frame with a margin of +0.455 over silent frames and zero false‑positives on blank frames (Llama‑3.2‑Vision 11B).
The same multimodal LLM (Llama‑4‑Scout 17B) falsely labels silent frames as speaking (10/12), exposing a hidden failure when a blank control is used.
Spectrogram‑to‑vision model (jev‑1.14.0) performs at chance on speaker‑change detection from spectrogram images (AUC ≈ 0.5).
The watcher’s per‑second CPU cost is correctly measured at ~39 % of a core on non‑speech fixtures (mean 39.13 ms per 100 ms of audio), not the undocumented 31.8 % figure.
On the single‑speaker LibriVox corpus, speaker‑change after a pause occurs < 2 % of the time; the system cannot learn turn‑taking from this data.

The character‑delta representation does **not** measure subject motion; it is dominated by camera auto‑exposure drift.
Composing row‑band removal with a temporal median reduces occupied‑scene flip rate to ≈0.0014 while empty‑room saturation remains ≈0.0348.
No usable pose signal is present in the 160×96 video frames.
A large multimodal model (Llama‑3.2‑Vision 11B) can detect speaking from a webcam frame with a margin of +0.455 over a silent control and zero false positives on blank frames.

The same multimodal model’s apparent perfect performance on the “blank” control hides a failure: Llama‑4‑Scout 17B reports speaking on 10/12 silent frames (margin = +0.167) and zero false positives on blank frames.
F0 jump size predicts speaker change only in one corpus cell (children), with a modest correlation (ρ = 0.341, p = 0.006).
Raising the VAD pause threshold from 150 ms to 200 ms discards 17.8 % of real pauses.
A 2‑order‑of‑magnitude high‑pass filter (200 Hz) attenuates mains hum but introduces negligible pitch error (median = 0.73 cents).
The documented 31.8 % CPU usage figure for the watcher was never measured; the only measured figure is 39.13 % core (≈39.13 ms per 100 ms of audio).
GATE_FIELD does not under‑report gate peaks; the earlier 14.5× understatement was due to comparing different intervals.

runs.title: Gate advantage under cache pressure on low‑memory targets

next_experiment.title: Gate advantage under cache pressure on low‑memory targets
next_experiment.hypothesis: On a Pi‑class device with ≤256 KB L2 cache, the Silero‑VAD gate will not retain its >10× CPU‑usage advantage over the ungated watcher.
next_experiment.method: Run the watcher on a Raspberry Pi 4 (2 MiB L2, 4 MiB L3) processing the same six benchmark signals (steady hum, fan, keyboard, music triad, white noise, near‑silence) for 30 s each. Measure CPU time via getrusage for (a) ungated watcher, (b) gated watcher, (c) a minimal YIN‑only baseline. Record warm runs (no cache flush) and cold runs (L1/L2/L3 flushed before each 100 ms chunk). Compute the ratio (ungated / gated) for both warm and cold conditions.
next_experiment.null: Ratio of ungated to gated CPU usage ≤ 1 (no advantage or inversion).
next_experiment.margin_threshold: The gated watcher must achieve a ≥ 2× reduction in CPU usage relative to the ungated watcher (ratio ≥ 2) in both warm and cold conditions.
next_experiment.falsifier: If the measured ratio is ≤ 1 in either warm or cold runs, the hypothesis is falsified and the gate cannot be relied upon for low‑memory devices.

unsafe_claims: The gate’s field threshold understates the gate by 14.5× because of a trimming bug.
The ASCII‑motion character delta measures subject motion (48.19 % vs 50 % empty).
The watcher’s cost is 31.8 % of a core (the “31.8 %” figure).
Gain normalisation cuts drift from 43.3 to 0.81 counts (≈50× reduction).
A local LLM can label speech from an ASCII rendering of the motion field.
The teacher scored 0.000 leave‑one‑out for every feature set.
state_of_the_evidence: A Silero‑VAD gate placed before the watcher reduces CPU usage by roughly an order of magnitude on the development workstation.
The current watcher misclassifies non‑speech signals as speech at a saturated 89 % rate.
The watcher’s per‑second CPU cost on this machine is ≈39 % of a core (≈39 ms per 100 ms of audio).
Row‑band removal combined with a 3‑frame temporal median reduces the occupied‑room flip rate from ≈3 % to ≈0.14 % while keeping empty‑room saturation low.
The character‑delta representation does not measure subject motion; it is dominated by camera auto‑exposure drift.
Gain normalisation does not reduce the drift of the character‑delta field.
F0 jump size predicts speaker change only for the ‘children’ cell; other cells show no significant effect.
No usable pose signal is present in the 160×96 video; the best feature (mirror_cov) shows a margin of +0.814 but is blind to head turn.
A large multimodal model (Llama‑3.2‑Vision‑11B) can detect speaking from a 160×96 webcam frame with a +0.455 margin over silent frames and zero false positives on blank frames.
Conventional teacher models achieve perfect training accuracy but fail completely on leave‑one‑session‑out validation (0 % accuracy).
